title: Quantum Pseudorandom Error-Correcting Codes
abstract: Pseudorandom error-correcting codes (PRCs), introduced by Christ and Gunn [CRYPTO 2024], are classical error-correcting codes whose codewords are computationally indistinguishable from uniformly random strings. We initiate the study of quantum analogues of PRCs. We define quantum pseudorandom error-correcting codes (QPRCs). Assuming that Learning Parity with Noise (LPN) is hard for $2^{O(\sqrt{n})}$-time quantum algorithms, we construct QPRCs whose encodings are indistinguishable from Haar-random isometries. We call these pseudorandom isometric error-correcting codes (PRICs), and our construction is robust to all $o(n \frac{\log \log n}{\log n})$-local quantum noise, where $n$ is the number of physical qubits. Under the same assumption, we also construct QPRCs whose encodings are indistinguishable from the completely depolarizing channel and that are robust to all $αn$-local quantum noise for some constant $α>0$. The latter QPRCs give a direct quantum analogue of classical PRCs.   To construct PRICs, we develop two technical ingredients of independent interest. First, we introduce a new classical cryptographic primitive which we call pseudorandom functional error-correcting codes (PRFCs) and construct them under the same LPN assumption. Second, we develop a new efficient decoding procedure within the codeword-stabilized (CWS) framework introduced in [Cross, Smith, Smolin, and Zeng, IEEE ISIT 2008], which is a generic framework for constructing quantum error-correcting codes by combining (possibly nonlinear) classical error-correcting codes and graphs. This resolves the open problem of finding a general method for efficiently decoding such CWS codes based on nonlinear classical codes, raised in [Li, Dumer, Grassl, and Pryadko, Physical Review A 2010].
summary: This paper introduces Quantum Pseudorandom Error-Correcting Codes (QPRCs) as quantum analogues of classical PRCs. By developing new classical tools and refining decoding methods, the authors construct PRICs that are provably robust to local quantum noise while remaining computationally indistinguishable from ideal random quantum states. This advances the field by merging quantum error correction with quantum cryptography.
main_problem: The paper aims to construct Quantum Pseudorandom Error-Correcting Codes (QPRCs) that are quantum analogues of classical PRCs, ensuring both strong pseudorandomness and robustness against local quantum noise.
main_result: The authors construct PRICs (Pseudorandom Isometric Error-Correcting Codes) robust to $o(n \log \log n / \log n)$-local quantum noise, achieving a direct quantum analogue of classical PRCs under the LPN assumption.
method: The construction relies on developing new classical primitives (PRFCs) and improving the decoding procedure within the Codeword-Stabilized (CWS) framework to build the quantum codes.
model_or_system: The model involves quantum error correction, encoding $n_L$ logical qubits into $n_P$ physical qubits, and analyzing the performance of the resulting quantum channels under local noise.
key_observables: The fidelity of the encoding/decoding process relative to the identity channel (diamond distance), and the distinguishability between the encoded state and ideal random states (Haar-random isometries).
important_parameters: The physical qubit number ($n_P$), the number of logical qubits ($n_L$), the local noise threshold ($t$ or $\alpha n$), and the security parameter $\lambda$.
main_assumptions: The hardness of the Learning Parity with Noise (LPN) problem for $2^{O(\sqrt{n})}$-time quantum algorithms is the primary assumption.
figures_summary: No specific figures are described, but the notes reference tables summarizing the capabilities of different code types (PRC, PRFC, QPRC, PRIC).
paper_structure: The paper develops the theory by first defining QPRCs, then constructing PRICs using new classical primitives (PRFCs) and advanced decoding techniques within the CWS framework, culminating in proofs bounding the error and distinguishing capabilities.
why_interesting: The work provides concrete, theoretically grounded constructions for quantum codes that possess desirable cryptographic properties (pseudorandomness) alongside their primary function (error correction), which is crucial for building secure quantum communication protocols.
